podcast.title: Comedy Central Promo Origin of Hate (2003)
podcast.body: One theory for the widespread hatred attributes its origin to a Comedy Central promo for the show "Tough Crowd," featuring Colin Quinn, which began airing on May 5, 2003. In the promo, Quinn humorously linked violent music to violent behavior, quipping that "bad music makes bad music," and specifically, "listening to Nickelback makes me want to kill Nickelback." This coincided with Nickelback's explosion in popularity with their "Silver Side Up" album and hit single "How You Remind Me." "For the answer, we probably have to go back to Comedy Central, the American TV channel, back in 2003. The channel ran a promo for a show called Tough Crowd featuring Colin Quinn. In this promo, he referenced a study that linked violent music to violent behavior. I quote, no one talks about the studies that show that bad music makes bad music. But listening to Nickelback makes me want to kill Nickelback."

podcast.body: Nickelback's album was the biggest selling rock record in 2006, achieving sales of 2.7 million copies. podcast.title: "Familiarity Bred Contempt" Theory
podcast.body: Following the Comedy Central promo in 2003, Nickelback continued to grow significantly in popularity, becoming increasingly ubiquitous. This theory suggests that their widespread presence and constant exposure led to "familiarity bred contempt," contributing to the intense and disproportionate hatred they received. "And Nickelback only got bigger and bigger and bigger over the coming years. And apparently familiarity bred contempt."

podcast.title: Authenticity Study and Perceived Genericism (University of Eastern Finland)
podcast.body: A study from the University of Eastern Finland, titled "Hipper Critical BS performed through Gritted Teeth, Authenticity Dis courses in Nickelback's album reviews and Finnish media," investigated the origins of the band's widespread hate. It concluded that critics perceived Nickelback as "not genuine enough," "too generic in their sound and their image," and simultaneously following genre expectations "too well" (seen as empty imitation) and "not well enough" (interpreted as commercial tactics and a lack of sincere identity). "According to critics, Nickelback isn't genuine enough. Plus they're too generic in their sound and their image. I quote, Nickelback is too much of everything to be enough of something. They follow genre expectations too well, which is seen as empty imitation. But also not well enough, which is read as commercial tactics and as a lack of a stable and sincere identity."

podcast.body: The name Nickelback originated from Mike Kruger's time working at Starbucks, where he frequently told customers, "Here's your Nickelback." "Mike Kruger used to work at Starbucks and found himself saying to everyone, here's your Nickelback."

This difference sometimes led to external pressure from others trying to impose Kroeger's methods on Ian's projects. "But the way that he works is very different than the way that I work."

podcast.title: Disproportionate Hatred and Radio Bans
podcast.body: Despite their substantial fanbase and commercial success, Nickelback faces an unusually high level of public disgust, hate, and a proliferation of anti-Nickelback memes. Some radio stations have even implemented "no Nickelback policies" due to this widespread negative sentiment. "Why the disproportionate amount of disgust and hate for them? Why all the haters? podcast.title: Hanna, Alberta Origins - Population 2,673
podcast.body: Nickelback hails from Hanna, Alberta, a town of 2,673 people located about two and a half hours northeast of Calgary. The town's official symbol is the Canada Grey Goose, which is featured in its logo. "Let's pause for a second to talk about Nickelback. From Hannah Alberta, a town of 2,673 people, about two and a half hours northeast of Calgary. Officially, this is the home of the Canada Grey Goose. podcast.title: Impact on Music Industry Ecosystem
podcast.body: Despite widespread criticism and "irrational global hatred," Nickelback is recognized as a vital component of the music industry's ecosystem. Their commercial success and high album sales meant they were a "hit band" that generated substantial profits. This revenue, particularly during their tenure with Roadrunner Records, was instrumental in subsidizing releases for numerous metal bands such as Opeth, Killswitch Engage, and Mastodon, and also provided crucial "seed money" for Billy Talent's entry into the US market. They exemplify the "rule of 30" in music, where a few highly successful acts financially support many others. "They are an important part of the music industry ecosystem."

podcast.title: Subject of "Irrational Hate"
podcast.body: Nickelback became the target of an "inexplicable and irrational amount of hate and ridicule," beginning in the early 2000s, possibly after comedian Colin Quinn's insult on Comedy Central which turned into a channel promo. Despite selling millions of albums, being extensively played on American radio (more than The Beatles), and selling hundreds of thousands of concert tickets, the band became a meme, a punchline, and shorthand for "bad music." This level of abuse was considered unwarranted. "As for number 64, I'm going to go with what I think was the inexplicable and irrational amount of hate and ridicule directed towards Nickelback."

xref.title: US Market Struggles (1990s onward)
xref.body: The Tragically Hip never achieved major stardom in the American market, a phenomenon that has become an area of study. While they have pockets of support, their timing often did not align with prevailing American rock trends. For instance, in the 1990s, American rock was dominated by grunge, then hip hop, and later indie rock (like The Strokes or The White Stripes), none of which perfectly matched the Hip's style. "Why has the tragically hip never been able to break through in the States? While this isn't entirely true, the hip do have pockets of support in America. But unlike Brian Adams or Lannis Morsehsett or Nickelback, it just seems that their timing was off. Their music was great, but whenever they were hot, American rock and roll attitudes were somewhere else. In the 90s, it was grunge, and the hip are not grunge. Then came hip hop. Hip didn't belong there. Then it was Indy Rock and the flavor of the strokes, so the white stripes and the hip didn't really fit in there either."
